supported_claims.text: 洗 is analyzed as a water-related phonosemantic compound: 氵 contributes the water category, and 先 is named as the sound element. An early lexicographic gloss gives its use as washing the feet.

The phonetic analysis is a historical source claim. In Baxter–Sagart 2014, 先 has Middle Chinese sen and Old Chinese *sˤər; 洗 has two listed readings, including Middle Chinese senX and Old Chinese *sˤərʔ. The dossier notes resemblance but does not establish that this comparison proves the component’s role.
The curated image is a modern drawing of 先 in Shuowen seal-script style. It illustrates the named component, not an early form of 洗.
The dossier documents 洗 for foot washing, washing ritual vessels, and a vessel associated with wash water. The cited textual examples do not establish a precise chronology among these uses.
The current meanings include washing or rinsing and cleaning or purifying; the dossier does not establish a linear development from foot washing to these broader senses.

The record reports later overlap between 洗 and 洒, including accounts in which 洒 was a variant or ancient form of 洗, and an account that 洗 later replaced 洒 for general washing. This does not establish 洒 as 洗’s original graphic form.

disagreements.text: An oracle-bone graph has been identified as 洗 by one cited scholar and as 歬 by another. A later proposal relates early forms to foot washing and proposes that 歬 was borrowed for ‘go forward,’ but the identification is disputed and the glyphs were not independently inspected.
The traditional analysis gives 洗 as water plus phonetic 先; a scholarly proposal instead discusses an early 洗/歬 relationship. The dossier does not resolve the paleographic disagreement.

limitations.text: No verified historical glyph image of 洗 is supplied, and the dossier does not settle the disputed oracle-bone identification or establish a secure early graphic sequence.

The paired readings allow a notation-specific sound comparison, but the dossier says this does not independently prove the ancient pronunciation or phonetic function of the graphic component. Current Mandarin readings xǐ and xiān likewise do not establish an ancient relationship.

The cited transmitted texts document separate uses but do not supply exact manuscript dates or establish the first attestation or a semantic sequence among foot washing, vessel-related uses, general washing, and purification.
The dossier advances no phonetic-loan account for 洗 and establishes no independently recoverable ancient object name for the disputed early graph.
